title: Spring AI 2.0.0 starters pull Spring Boot 4.1.0 dependencies despite documented Spring Boot 4.0.x compatibility
body:
# Spring AI 2.0.0 starters pull Spring Boot 4.1.0 dependencies despite documented Spring Boot 4.0.x compatibility

## Bug description

Spring AI 2.0.x documentation states that Spring AI 2.0.x supports both Spring Boot 4.0.x and 4.1.x.

However, the released Spring AI 2.0.0 starter artifacts are aligned with Spring Boot 4.1.0 dependency versions. When an application is intentionally based on Spring Boot 4.0.x and imports the Spring AI 2.0.0 BOM as documented, adding an official Spring AI starter can introduce Spring Boot 4.1.0 dependency requests into the Maven dependency graph.

The attached minimal reproducer demonstrates this with:

- Spring Boot parent: `4.0.7`
- Spring AI BOM: `2.0.0`
- Spring AI starter: `spring-ai-starter-model-mistral-ai`
- Java: `21`
- Maven Enforcer: `dependencyConvergence` and `requireUpperBoundDeps`

## Why this matters

Our platform parent is intentionally fixed to Spring Boot 4.0.7 because we are in the middle of a larger Spring Boot 4 migration and have other platform components that cannot yet move to Spring Boot 4.1.x.

For such enterprise platforms, the consuming application's Spring Boot parent/BOM must remain authoritative for Spring Boot-managed dependency versions.

If Spring AI 2.0.x is documented as supporting Spring Boot 4.0.x and 4.1.x, official Spring AI 2.0.0 starters should not force or request Spring Boot 4.1.0-level dependencies in a Spring Boot 4.0.x application.

## Reproducer

The attached project contains two POMs:

- `pom.xml` — failing Spring Boot `4.0.7` case
- `pom-boot-410.xml` — passing Spring Boot `4.1.0` control case

Both use the same Spring AI setup:

```xml
<properties>
    <spring-ai.version>2.0.0</spring-ai.version>
</properties>

<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.ai</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-ai-bom</artifactId>
            <version>${spring-ai.version}</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.ai</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-ai-starter-model-mistral-ai</artifactId>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>
```

Both POMs enable:

```xml
<dependencyConvergence />
<requireUpperBoundDeps />
```

## Steps to reproduce

### Failing Spring Boot 4.0.7 case

```bash
mvn validate
```

Observed result:

```text
Rule 0: org.apache.maven.enforcer.rules.dependency.DependencyConvergence passed
Rule 1: org.apache.maven.enforcer.rules.dependency.RequireUpperBoundDeps failed
BUILD FAILURE
```

Relevant failures:

```text
Require upper bound dependencies error for org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-restclient:4.0.7. Paths to dependency are:
+-com.example:spring-ai-boot-407-reproducer:0.0.1-SNAPSHOT
  +-org.springframework.ai:spring-ai-starter-model-mistral-ai:2.0.0
    +-org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-restclient:4.0.7 (managed) <-- org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-restclient:4.1.0

Require upper bound dependencies error for org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-webclient:4.0.7. Paths to dependency are:
+-com.example:spring-ai-boot-407-reproducer:0.0.1-SNAPSHOT
  +-org.springframework.ai:spring-ai-starter-model-mistral-ai:2.0.0
    +-org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-webclient:4.0.7 (managed) <-- org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-webclient:4.1.0

Require upper bound dependencies error for io.micrometer:micrometer-core:1.16.6. Paths to dependency are:
+-com.example:spring-ai-boot-407-reproducer:0.0.1-SNAPSHOT
  +-org.springframework.ai:spring-ai-starter-model-mistral-ai:2.0.0
    +-org.springframework.ai:spring-ai-mistral-ai:2.0.0 (managed) <-- org.springframework.ai:spring-ai-mistral-ai:2.0.0
      +-org.springframework.ai:spring-ai-model:2.0.0 (managed) <-- org.springframework.ai:spring-ai-model:2.0.0
        +-org.springframework.ai:spring-ai-commons:2.0.0 (managed) <-- org.springframework.ai:spring-ai-commons:2.0.0
          +-io.micrometer:micrometer-core:1.16.6 (managed) <-- io.micrometer:micrometer-core:1.17.0

Require upper bound dependencies error for io.micrometer:micrometer-observation:1.16.6. Paths to dependency are:
+-com.example:spring-ai-boot-407-reproducer:0.0.1-SNAPSHOT
  +-org.springframework.ai:spring-ai-starter-model-mistral-ai:2.0.0
    +-org.springframework.ai:spring-ai-mistral-ai:2.0.0 (managed) <-- org.springframework.ai:spring-ai-mistral-ai:2.0.0
      +-org.springframework.ai:spring-ai-model:2.0.0 (managed) <-- org.springframework.ai:spring-ai-model:2.0.0
        +-io.micrometer:micrometer-observation:1.16.6 (managed) <-- io.micrometer:micrometer-observation:1.17.0
```

The full captured output is included in `FAILURE-boot-407-enforcer.md`.

### Passing Spring Boot 4.1.0 control case

```bash
mvn clean install -f pom-boot-410.xml
```

Observed result:

```text
Rule 0: org.apache.maven.enforcer.rules.dependency.DependencyConvergence passed
Rule 1: org.apache.maven.enforcer.rules.dependency.RequireUpperBoundDeps passed
BUILD SUCCESS
```

## Expected behavior

A Spring Boot 4.0.x application using the official Spring AI 2.0.0 BOM and official Spring AI starter dependencies should not receive Spring Boot 4.1.0-level dependency requests from Spring AI starters.

The consuming application's Spring Boot parent/BOM should remain authoritative for Spring Boot-managed dependency versions.

## Actual behavior

With Spring Boot 4.0.7 and Spring AI 2.0.0, Maven Enforcer reports upper-bound dependency failures because Spring AI 2.0.0 requests dependencies aligned with Spring Boot 4.1.0 / Micrometer 1.17.0, while the Spring Boot 4.0.7 parent manages them to Boot 4.0.7 / Micrometer 1.16.6 versions.

## Suggested solutions

One of the following would make the compatibility story safer and clearer:

1. Avoid hard-coding Spring Boot starter versions in Spring AI starter POMs and let the consuming application's Spring Boot BOM manage them.

2. Provide separate compatibility lines or release trains, similar to Spring Cloud, so that users can clearly select a Spring AI line aligned with Spring Boot 4.0.x or Spring Boot 4.1.x.

3. Alternatively, update the documentation to clarify that Spring AI 2.0.0 core libraries may work with Spring Boot 4.0.x, but the published Spring AI 2.0.0 starters are aligned with Spring Boot 4.1.0 and may require dependency-management overrides or avoiding starters in Spring Boot 4.0.x applications.

## Related documentation / release notes

- Spring AI reference documentation currently states: “Spring AI 2.0.x supports Spring Boot 4.0.x and 4.1.x.”
  https://docs.spring.io/spring-ai/reference/getting-started.html

- Spring AI 2.0.0 GA announcement states that Spring AI 2.0 has been designed to be used with Spring Boot 4.0 / 4.1 and Spring Framework 7.0.
  https://spring.io/blog/2026/06/12/spring-ai-2-0-0-GA-available-now/

- Spring AI 2.0.0 release notes list “Upgrade Spring Boot 4.1.0”.
  https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-ai/releases/tag/v2.0.0

[spring-ai-boot-407-reproducer.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29132599/spring-ai-boot-407-reproducer.zip)

comments.author: uweguenther
comments.body:
Thanks, I think we are looking at two different layers here.

I agree with you that the final resolved application is using Boot 4.0.7.

For example:

- dependency:tree shows Boot 4.0.7
- effective-pom shows Boot 4.0.7
- the packaged jar contains Boot 4.0.7 libraries

So Maven dependency management is working correctly.

The issue I am trying to point out is one layer earlier:

The Spring AI 2.0.0 starter POMs still request Boot 4.1.0 dependencies.

Example:

spring-ai-starter-model-mistral-ai:2.0.0
-> spring-boot-starter-webclient:4.1.0
-> spring-boot-starter-restclient:4.1.0

In a Boot 4.0.7 application, Maven then manages those requests down to 4.0.7.

That gives this Enforcer output:

spring-boot-starter-webclient:4.0.7 (managed) <-- spring-boot-starter-webclient:4.1.0
spring-boot-starter-restclient:4.0.7 (managed) <-- spring-boot-starter-restclient:4.1.0

So the problem is not:

"Boot 4.1.0 ends up in the jar"

The problem is:

"The published Spring AI 2.0.0 starter metadata asks for Boot 4.1.0, even in a documented Boot 4.0.x compatible line."

For teams using strict platform builds, this matters because Enforcer is used to detect exactly this kind of version drift.

So yes, the final resolved version is correct.

But Enforcer is exposing that Spring AI 2.0.0 was published from / aligned with a Boot 4.1.0 dependency baseline.

The question is:

If Spring AI 2.0.x supports Boot 4.0.x, should the published starter POMs avoid hard Boot 4.1.0 dependency requests?

Or should the documentation say that the 2.0.0 starters are Boot 4.1.0 aligned, and Boot 4.0.x users may need local dependency-management/exclusion workarounds?

@ericbottard @jewoodev  One additional data point:

This was working for us up to Spring AI 2.0.0-M2.

With 2.0.0-M2, the Spring AI starter metadata was still aligned closely enough with a Spring Boot 4.0.x application that our strict Enforcer setup did not report the Boot 4.1.0 / Micrometer 1.17.0 upper-bound conflicts.

The problem appears after the baseline moved toward Spring Boot 4.1.x.

So from a consumer perspective the regression is:

- Spring AI 2.0.0-M2 + Spring Boot 4.0.x: works with strict Enforcer
- Spring AI 2.0.0 GA + Spring Boot 4.0.x: fails with strict Enforcer because the published starter POMs request Boot 4.1.0 / Micrometer 1.17.0 artifacts

Hi @ericbottard,

thanks, that makes sense.

I agree that from a casual user perspective there may be no visible problem, because Maven dependency management resolves the final application artifacts to the Boot version managed by the consuming application.

The place where this becomes visible is platform governance / strict build validation.

* final resolved/runtime compatibility, and
* published POM metadata being clean against the lowest supported Boot baseline.

For enterprise users, this distinction matters because the Spring Boot version is usually centrally managed by a platform parent, and Enforcer is intentionally used to detect dependency drift before it reaches applications.

comments.author: pkubowicz
comments.body:
This is not a problem with Maven. It's a problem of Spring AI publishing wrong metadata. Any build tool expecting sane POM will be able to get into a problem.

Here I can reproduce a similar problem with Gradle:

```
dependencies {
    api(platform("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-dependencies:4.0.7"))
    api(platform("org.springframework.ai:spring-ai-bom:2.0.0"))
    implementation("org.springframework.ai:spring-ai-starter-mcp-server-webmvc")
    implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-autoconfigure")
    implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-health")
}
```

```shell
gradle depIns --configuration=runCl --dependency=spring-boot-autoconfigure
```

In this simple project, 4.1.0 is used for some dependencies (like spring-boot or sprint-boot-autoconfigure) but not for others (4.0.7 for spring-boot-health), as result of https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/org/springframework/ai/spring-ai-starter-mcp-server-webmvc/2.0.0/spring-ai-starter-mcp-server-webmvc-2.0.0.pom

Putting 4.1.0 into Spring AI POM is effectively like Spring AI saying 'I know better than you which Spring Boot version you need'. It takes lots of hacks (excluding, enforcing) to achieve a simple thing ('I declare I want Spring Boot 4.0 -> I get Spring Boot 4.0'), because of dependency tree poisoning.

If Spring Boot 4.0 is your lower bound of supported dependencies, you should put 4.0 into your POM - then at least I know your code compiles with Spring Boot 4.0. Now the POM says Spring AI works with SB 4.1, but it gives an impression it's hazardous to use that library with SB 4.0.

title: MilvusVectorStore filters ignore configured metadata field name
body:
**Bug description**

`MilvusVectorStore` supports configuring the metadata field name through `metadataFieldName(...)` and `spring.ai.vectorstore.milvus.metadata-field-name`.

However, filters still use the default `metadata` field. For example, with `metadataFieldName("meta")`, a filter expression such as `age > 30` is converted to:

```text
metadata["age"] > 30
```

The generated filter should use the configured metadata field name instead:

```text
meta["age"] > 30
```

As a result, filtered searches fail for Milvus collections that use a custom metadata field name.

**Environment**

- Spring AI version: `2.0.0`
- Java version: 21
- Vector store: Milvus

**Steps to reproduce**

1. Create a `MilvusVectorStore` with a custom metadata field name:

```java
MilvusVectorStore vectorStore = MilvusVectorStore.builder(milvusClient, embeddingModel)
	.metadataFieldName("meta")
	.build();
```

2. Run a similarity search with a Spring AI filter expression:

```java
SearchRequest request = SearchRequest.builder()
	.query("sample query")
	.filterExpression("age > 30")
	.build();

vectorStore.similaritySearch(request);
```

3. Inspect the generated Milvus `SearchParam` expression.

Actual expression:

```text
metadata["age"] > 30
```

When the same scenario is run against a real Milvus container, the search fails because the Milvus collection uses the custom `meta` field, not the default `metadata` field:

```text
failed to create query plan: cannot parse expression: metadata["age"] > 30, error: field metadata not exist: invalid parameter
```

**Expected behavior**

The generated Milvus filter expression should use the configured metadata field name:

```text
meta["age"] > 30
```

title: reasoning_content from OpenAI compatible providers is lost in streaming responses
body: ## Description When using OpenAI-compatible providers that return reasoning content through streaming deltas, the reasoning data is lost during Spring AI's chunk aggregation process. I reproduced this with DashScope Qwen3.6 Plus and deepseek-v4-flash. The provider returns: ```json { "choices": [ { "delta": { "reasoning_content": "thinking..." } } ] } ``` ### The OpenAI Java SDK correctly parses it into: ```java cccc.delta()._additionalProperties() ``` ### Example: ```java Choice{ delta=Delta{ additionalProperties={ reasoning_content='thinking...' } } } ``` ### However, in: ```java ChunkMerger.chunkToChatCompletion(...) ``` only content, refusal and toolCalls are copied into ChatCompletionMessage. The delta additional properties are discarded. Current code: ```java ChatCompletionMessage.Builder msgBuilder = ChatCompletionMessage.builder() .content(cccc.delta().content()) .refusal(cccc.delta().refusal()); ``` Later Spring AI tries to read: ```java choice.message()._additionalProperties() ``` inside: ```java getReasoningContent(...) ``` but the properties are already lost. ## Suggested Fix Copy delta additional properties into ChatCompletionMessage. Example: ```java cccc.delta() ._additionalProperties() .forEach(msgBuilder::putAdditionalProperty); ``` This allows existing reasoning_content support in: ```java getReasoningContent(...) ``` to work correctly. Verified locally. After preserving delta additional properties, reasoningContent is correctly populated. ## Version ** Spring AI 2.0.0-RC2** I have already submitted a pull request containing the fix. https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-ai/pull/6483

title: Add `functionCallingConfig` / tool-choice mode support to `GoogleGenAiChatOptions`
body:
## Problem

`GoogleGenAiChatOptions` has no way to control function calling mode (the Gemini-native equivalent of OpenAI's `tool_choice`). When a request comes in with `tool_choice` set, there is no path to forward that intent to the underlying model — it has to be silently dropped.

## The SDK already supports it

`com.google.genai` v1.58.0 (the version currently used by Spring AI) exposes `ToolConfig.functionCallingConfig`, which accepts a `FunctionCallingConfig` with a `mode` field: `AUTO`, `ANY`, `NONE`, `VALIDATED`. This maps directly to OpenAI's `tool_choice` values. Spring AI just hasn't wired it up.

## Suggested solution

Add a `functionCallingMode` (and optionally `allowedFunctionNames` for `ANY` mode) to `GoogleGenAiChatOptions`, and have `GoogleGenAiChatModel` pass it through to `ToolConfig.functionCallingConfig` when building the `GenerateContentConfig`.

For reference: OpenAI's `tool_choice` is already mapped via `OpenAiChatOptions` and Anthropic's via `AnthropicChatOptions` — this would bring `GoogleGenAiChatOptions` to parity.

comments.body:
Hi, I'd like to work on this if no one else has started.

Proposed approach:
- Add a `GoogleGenAiFunctionCallingMode` enum (AUTO/ANY/NONE/VALIDATED) in the `common` package, mirroring `GoogleGenAiThinkingLevel`.
- Add `functionCallingMode` and an optional `allowedFunctionNames` fields to `GoogleGenAiChatOptions` (following the existing `thinkingLevel` field pattern: field, constructor, getters, equals/hashCode, builder, mutate()).
- In `GoogleGenAiChatModel`, wire these into `ToolConfig.functionCallingConfig(...)` using the SDK's `FunctionCallingConfig` (google-genai 1.58.0), merging with the existing `includeServerSideToolInvocations` ToolConfig rather than creating a separate one. I verified the SDK accepts `FunctionCallingConfig.builder().mode(String)` via case-insensitive matching against `FunctionCallingConfigMode.Known`, so passing the enum name works directly.
- Add unit tests in `GoogleGenAiChatOptionsTest`.


Let me know if this direction works and I'll open a PR.

title: `TokenCountBatchingStrategy` silently drops equal documents from batches
body:
**Bug description**

`TokenCountBatchingStrategy.batch(List<Document>)` collects per-document token
counts into a `Map<Document, Integer>` before forming batches. Since
`Document.equals()` compares id, text, media, metadata and score, two equal
documents collapse into a single map entry, so the duplicate is silently
dropped from the returned batches.

`batch` is a partitioning operation, and its only caller,
`EmbeddingModel.embed(List<Document>, ...)`, maps the returned embeddings back
to the input documents by position and asserts
`embeddings.size() == documents.size()`. When a duplicate is dropped, the
provider returns fewer embeddings than input documents and ingestion fails
with:

```
IllegalArgumentException: Embeddings must have the same number as that of the documents
```

which points at the embedding provider rather than the batching step.

This happens in practice with content-based id generators (e.g.
`JdkSha256HexIdGenerator`), where identical chunks such as repeated
boilerplate produce equal `Document`s, and trivially when the same `Document`
instance appears twice in the list.

**Environment**

Reproduced on Spring AI `main`. Plain JVM, no provider involved 
the failing path is entirely within `TokenCountBatchingStrategy`, so it
reproduces offline.

**Steps to reproduce**

```java
TokenCountBatchingStrategy strategy = new TokenCountBatchingStrategy();
Document d1 = new Document("shared-id", "same text content", Map.of());
Document d2 = new Document("shared-id", "same text content", Map.of());

List<List<Document>> batches = strategy.batch(List.of(d1, d2));
// batches contain 1 document in total, not 2
```

The same happens with `strategy.batch(List.of(d1, d1))`.

**Expected behavior**

`batch` preserves every input document, regardless of document equality.
Deduplication policy, if desired, belongs to the ingestion layer that owns
document identity, not to the token-count partitioner.

title: Per-call `customHeaders` not propagated in `OpenAiEmbeddingOptions`
body:
> **A note before the report:** I'm not a native English speaker, so I drafted
> this issue with the help of an LLM to describe the problem as precisely as I
> could. Apologies for any awkward phrasing, and thank you for your understanding.

**Bug description**

`OpenAiEmbeddingOptions#customHeaders` set on a per-`EmbeddingRequest` basis are
never applied to the outgoing OpenAI embeddings request. `OpenAiEmbeddingOptions#toOpenAiCreateParams(...)`
builds the `EmbeddingCreateParams` from only `model` / `input` / `user` /
`encodingFormat` / `dimensions`, and never consumes `getCustomHeaders()`:

```java
// OpenAiEmbeddingOptions#toOpenAiCreateParams (main, 2.0.1-SNAPSHOT)
public EmbeddingCreateParams toOpenAiCreateParams(List<String> instructions) {
    EmbeddingCreateParams.Builder builder = EmbeddingCreateParams.builder();
    // ... model / input / user / encodingFormat / dimensions ...
    return builder.build();   // customHeaders never applied
}
```

The map is only consumed once, when the underlying `OpenAIClient` is built in
`OpenAiSetup.setupSyncClient(...)`. So when an `OpenAIClient` is injected
directly into `OpenAiEmbeddingModel`, headers configured at runtime (per call)
are silently dropped.

This is inconsistent with:
- the **chat** side (`OpenAiChatModel#createRequest`), which propagates per-call
  `customHeaders` to `ChatCompletionCreateParams` via `putAdditionalHeader`
  (added in `2.0.0-M5`, commit f36dce3), and
- the **image** side, which had the exact same bug and was already fixed in
  #6082 / #6083 (`OpenAiImageOptions` now calls
  `getCustomHeaders().forEach(builder::putAdditionalHeader)`).

Embedding is the remaining OpenAI model type where per-call `customHeaders` are
still dropped.

**Use case affected**

Calling LLM-gateway proxies that require a per-request header derived from the
business request (e.g. a distributed-tracing / correlation header such as
`trace-id`). A static client-level header is not sufficient, because a single
embedding model/client is shared across many callers. This is the same
motivation described in #6082 for images.

**Environment**

- Spring AI: `main` (verified on commit ac8b2da26, `2.0.1-SNAPSHOT`)
- module: `spring-ai-openai`

**Steps to reproduce**

```java
EmbeddingResponse resp = openAiEmbeddingModel.call(new EmbeddingRequest(
    List.of("hello world"),
    OpenAiEmbeddingOptions.builder()
        .model("text-embedding-3-small")
        .customHeaders(Map.of("trace-id", "TRACE_123"))
        .build()));
```

Inspect the outgoing HTTP request (`OPENAI_LOG=debug`). The `trace-id` header
is **not** present on the `/v1/embeddings` call.

**Expected behavior**

Per-call `customHeaders` should be propagated as `additionalHeaders` on the
`EmbeddingCreateParams` sent to `openAiClient.embeddings().create(...)`,
consistent with chat (`OpenAiChatModel#createRequest`) and image (#6082/#6083).

**Suggested fix**

Mirror the image fix (#6083) in `OpenAiEmbeddingOptions#toOpenAiCreateParams`:

```java
if (!CollectionUtils.isEmpty(this.getCustomHeaders())) {
    this.getCustomHeaders().forEach(builder::putAdditionalHeader);
}
```

title: AnthropicChatOptions.timeout(Duration) set via ChatClient (default or per-request) is silently ignored — only construction-time timeout applies
body:
Please do a quick search on GitHub issues first, there might be already a duplicate issue for the one you are about to create.
If the bug is trivial, just go ahead and create the issue. Otherwise, please take a few moments and fill in the following sections:

**Bug description**

The official docs show this as valid, working usage:

```java
var chatOptions = AnthropicChatOptions.builder()
    .model("claude-sonnet-4-20250514")
    .maxTokens(1024)
    .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(120))
    .build();
```

**We followed this exact documented pattern** — set `.timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(N))` via `ChatClient.Builder.defaultOptions()` and via per-request `ChatClient.prompt().options(...)` — and it did not work. The configured `Duration` is silently accepted (no error, no warning) but has **zero effect** on the actual HTTP timeout used for the call.

The *only* place a `timeout` Duration actually takes effect is `AnthropicChatModel` **construction time** — i.e. the `spring.ai.anthropic.timeout` property, consumed once by `AnthropicChatAutoConfiguration` when it builds the shared `AnthropicChatModel` bean. Nothing set afterwards — not `ChatClient.Builder.defaultOptions()`, not a per-request `ChatClient.prompt().options(...)` override — has any effect, contrary to what the docs show.

**Practical impact**: because the Anthropic SDK retries transient failures up to `maxRetries` (default 2, so 3 total attempts), an unconfigured/short construction-time timeout compounds silently: with the SDK's `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT` (60s) and no `spring.ai.anthropic.timeout` set, any call that legitimately needs more than 60s (e.g. `web_search` tool use, large `maxTokens` generations) reliably fails after ~180s (3 × 60s) — no matter what `AnthropicChatOptions.timeout(...)` is set via `ChatClient`, following the documented pattern exactly.

**Environment**

- Spring AI version: 2.0.0 (confirmed still present on `main` as of this report)
- Module: `spring-ai-anthropic`, `spring-ai-autoconfigure-model-anthropic`
- Java 21

**Steps to reproduce**

1. Start a local HTTP server that responds to `POST /v1/messages` after a fixed delay (e.g. 2s), returning a minimal valid `Message` JSON body.
2. Build an `AnthropicChatModel` with a **short** construction-time timeout (e.g. 500ms) — deliberately too short for the delayed response above.
3. Call it through `ChatClient` with a **longer** per-request timeout (e.g. 5s), exactly as documented — this should legitimately allow the 2s-delayed mock response to succeed.

See **Minimal Complete Reproducible example** below for the exact code.

**Expected behavior**

Per the documented example, the per-request `.timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))` should apply, and the call should succeed after ~2s (mock server delay < 5s per-request timeout).

**Actual behavior**

The call fails at ~500ms × 3 attempts — the construction-time 500ms timeout is used for every attempt; the per-request 5s value is completely ignored. Confirmed via an `AnthropicHttpClientBuilderCustomizer` interceptor logging the live `chain.readTimeoutMillis()`/`chain.call().timeout()` at call time: it consistently reports the construction-time value (500ms), never the per-request value (5000ms), across all 3 retry attempts.

**Minimal Complete Reproducible example**

```java
try (MockWebServer server = new MockWebServer()) {
    server.enqueue(new MockResponse().setHeadersDelay(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
        .setResponseCode(200)
        .setHeader("Content-Type", "application/json")
        .setBody("""
            {"id":"msg-test","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"ok"}],"model":"claude-haiku-4-5-20251001","stop_reason":"end_turn","usage":{"input_tokens":1,"output_tokens":1}}
            """));
    server.start();

    AnthropicChatModel chatModel = AnthropicChatModel.builder()
        .options(AnthropicChatOptions.builder()
            .baseUrl(server.url("/").toString())
            .apiKey("test-key")
            .model("claude-haiku-4-5-20251001")
            .maxTokens(10)
            .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(500)) // short construction-time timeout
            .build())
        .build();
    ChatClient chatClient = ChatClient.builder(chatModel).build();

    // Per the docs, this 5s per-request timeout should let the 2s-delayed call
    // succeed. Instead, it's ignored and the call fails at ~500ms.
    String content = chatClient.prompt()
        .user("hello")
        .options(AnthropicChatOptions.builder().timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5)))
        .call()
        .content();
}
```

**Root cause (traced via bytecode + source)**

`AnthropicChatAutoConfiguration.anthropicChatModel(...)` only threads `AnthropicConnectionProperties.timeout` (the `spring.ai.anthropic.timeout` property) into the `AnthropicChatOptions` used to build the shared `AnthropicChatModel` bean, once, at startup:

```java
if (connectionProperties.getTimeout() != null) {
    builder.timeout(connectionProperties.getTimeout());
}
...
var chatModel = AnthropicChatModel.builder().options(options)...build();
```

But `AnthropicChatModel.internalCall()`/`internalStream()` (the per-call path used by every `ChatClient` request) never reads the merged runtime `AnthropicChatOptions.getTimeout()` to build a per-call `com.anthropic.core.RequestOptions` — it always calls `messageService.withRawResponse().create(request)` / `createStreaming(request)` (no explicit `RequestOptions` argument), so `RequestOptions.none()` is used, and the actual HTTP client behavior is whatever was baked into the shared `AnthropicClient` at construction time.

**Fix**

We have a working fix + regression tests: #6605.

Related: #512 (general HTTP client configuration umbrella issue) and #4970 (open PR adding `connect-timeout`/`read-timeout` config *properties*, still construction-time-only) don't cover this specific case.

comments.author: seeun0210
comments.body: For context, related-but-distinct issues found while searching for duplicates: #4103 (general feature request for ChatClient-level timeout support, provider-agnostic — doesn't seem aware Anthropic already has a documented `AnthropicChatOptions.timeout(Duration)` that's simply not wired through) and #512 (general HTTP client configuration umbrella). Neither covers this specific case: an existing, documented, provider-specific timeout option that's silently ignored outside model construction.

comments.author: seeun0210
comments.body: Also checked closed issues and related open PRs — nothing duplicates this exact case. #4970 (open PR, adds `connect-timeout`/`read-timeout` config *properties* for several providers including Anthropic) is adjacent but doesn't fix this: it's still a construction-time-only mechanism, so the documented per-call `AnthropicChatOptions.timeout(Duration)` pattern this issue is about would remain silently ignored even with that PR merged.

title: OpenAI rate-limit metadata is always EmptyRateLimit in Spring AI 2.0.0
body:
**Bug description**

When using the OpenAI chat model with Spring AI 2.0.0, the rate-limit metadata returned by ChatResponse is always an instance of EmptyRateLimit.

The completion, model metadata, and token usage are populated correctly, but the OpenAI rate-limit response headers do not appear to be mapped to ChatResponseMetadata.

I believe rate-limit metadata was available in earlier Spring AI 2.0.0 milestone versions, possibly up to 2.0.0-M1, but it is no longer available in the final 2.0.0 release.

**Environment**

Spring AI: 2.0.0
OpenAI chat model
Model: gpt-5-mini-2025-08-07
Java: 21

**Steps to reproduce**

```
ChatResponse chatResponse = chatClient.prompt()
        .user("Which country has the largest population in Europe?")
        .call()
        .chatResponse();

log.info("completion = {}", chatResponse.getResult().getOutput().getText());

log.info("model = {}", chatResponse.getMetadata().getModel());

var usage = chatResponse.getMetadata().getUsage();
log.info("usage = {}", usage);

var rateLimit = chatResponse.getMetadata().getRateLimit();
log.info("rateLimit = {}", rateLimit);
```

The completion, model, and usage information are returned correctly.

```
model = gpt-5-mini-2025-08-07
usage = DefaultUsage{
    promptTokens=20,
    completionTokens=655,
    totalTokens=675,
    cacheReadInputTokens=0
}
rateLimit = org.springframework.ai.chat.metadata.EmptyRateLimit@24eecabf
```
chatResponse.getMetadata().getRateLimit() always returns EmptyRateLimit.

**Expected behavior**

The OpenAI rate-limit response headers should be mapped to `ChatResponseMetadata`, allowing request and token limits, remaining values, and reset times to be accessed through `getRateLimit()`.

title: OpenAiChatModel incorrectly sets finishReason to _UNKNOWN for intermediate streaming ChatResponse chunks
body:
**Bug description**
When streaming chat completions from OpenAI, OpenAiChatModel.ChunkMerger.chunkToChatCompletion() incorrectly sets the finishReason to `_UNKNOWN` for streaming responses with `"finish_reason": null`

**Environment**
Spring AI version: 2.0.0
Java version: 21
Spring Boot version: 4.0.7
OpenAI Java SDK version: 4.39.1 (shipped with Spring AI)

**Steps to reproduce**
1. Call chatClient.prompt(prompt).stream().chatResponse()
2. Inspect the value returned by ChatResponse.getResult().getMetadata().getFinishReason()
3. Observe that every intermediate streaming chunk has finishReason == "_UNKNOWN"

**Expected behavior**
For intermediate streaming chunks, finishReason should be null (unset). It should only be populated on the final chunk when the OpenAI API provides a value.

**Root cause in code:**
https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-ai/blob/0df8a450aed810d99eb08c0d7d581f14e2c05db4/models/spring-ai-openai/src/main/java/org/springframework/ai/openai/OpenAiChatModel.java#L1150
```
choiceBuilder.finishReason(ChatCompletion.Choice.FinishReason.of(""));
cccc.finishReason()
	.ifPresent(finishReason -> choiceBuilder.finishReason(ChatCompletion.Choice.FinishReason
	.of(finishReason.value().name().toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT))));
```
The current implementation:

1. Initializes finishReason with an empty string ("").
2. FinishReason.of("") resolves to FinishReason._UNKNOWN.
3. Only replaces the value when cccc.finishReason() is present
As a result, all intermediate streaming chunks having `"finish_reason": null` end up with _UNKNOWN instead of null.

comments.author: guanxuc
comments.body: This is indeed a difference between 2.x and 1.x. However, for the `openai-java` SDK, this approach aligns with its intended design.

comments.author: lexum-gegiyag
comments.body:
@guanxuc, thank you for the prompt response.

I believe there is an inconsistency introduced during the mapping from openai-java to Spring AI.

For intermediate streaming chunks, OpenAI's Choice.finishReason() returns Optional.empty(), indicating that the chunk does not yet have a finish reason. Only the final chunk in the stream is expected to contain a value, for example:
```
..., null, null, null, stop
```
However, after mapping to ChatResponse, the values become:
```
..., _UNKNOWN, _UNKNOWN, _UNKNOWN, STOP
```
My understanding is that the design intent is for finishReason to remain unset (Optional.empty()/null) for intermediate chunks, since this attribute is only meaningful for the final chunk. Mapping a missing value to _UNKNOWN changes the semantics: _UNKNOWN suggests that an unrecognized finish reason was received, whereas in reality no finish reason was provided at all.

title: MarkdownCodeBlockCleaner.clean() throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException on degenerate fence-only input
body:
## Component
`org.springframework.ai.converter.MarkdownCodeBlockCleaner`
File: `spring-ai-model/src/main/java/org/springframework/ai/converter/MarkdownCodeBlockCleaner.java`

## Spring AI version
Checked against `main` (commit `fb51ef2`, as of 2026-07-17).

## Describe the bug
`clean(String)` does not guard against negative lengths when stripping the
trailing fence on a single-line input. For input strings that are *only*
backticks (3 to 5 of them), `text.startsWith("```")` and `text.endsWith("```")`
are both `true` simultaneously (the fence characters overlap), so the method
proceeds into the single-line branch and eventually calls:

```java
text = text.substring(0, text.length() - 3);
```

When `text.length() - 3` is negative, this throws
`StringIndexOutOfBoundsException` instead of returning something sane (e.g.
the original text, or an empty string).

## Steps to reproduce
```java
MarkdownCodeBlockCleaner cleaner = new MarkdownCodeBlockCleaner();
cleaner.clean("```");
cleaner.clean("````");
cleaner.clean("`````");
cleaner.clean("``````");
```

Verified output (JDK 21.0.11, logic extracted verbatim from `clean()`):
```
INPUT: ```     ->  THROWS: java.lang.StringIndexOutOfBoundsException: Range [0, -3) out of bounds for length 0
INPUT: ````    ->  THROWS: java.lang.StringIndexOutOfBoundsException: Range [0, -2) out of bounds for length 1
INPUT: `````   ->  THROWS: java.lang.StringIndexOutOfBoundsException: Range [0, -1) out of bounds for length 2
INPUT: ``````  ->  OUTPUT: [] (does not throw)
```

## Expected behavior
The cleaner should handle degenerate/malformed fence-only input gracefully
(e.g. return the input unchanged, or an empty string) rather than throwing an
unchecked exception. Since `clean()` is typically invoked on raw LLM output,
a malformed or truncated response from a model could trigger this at
runtime in application code that doesn't expect it.

## Actual behavior
`StringIndexOutOfBoundsException` is thrown for 3-, 4-, and 5-backtick-only
inputs.

## Additional context
I extracted the `clean()` logic verbatim from the current `main` branch source
and ran it standalone under a real JDK 21 to confirm the above output — this
isn't a theoretical trace, it's actual reproduced behavior. I have not yet
run it through the module's own Maven build/test suite (just an isolated
JVM run of the identical logic), so I'm happy to be corrected if there's
context I'm missing, or if this overlaps with prior triage.

I'd like to submit a fix + accompanying unit tests for this if it's
confirmed and not already tracked elsewhere. Let me know if this overlaps
with prior work (e.g. #6403) or if there's a preferred approach (early
return vs. defensive length check).

body:
**Bug description**
Spring AI always creates a text content block from user messages that are sent to AWS Bedrock Converse API, even if the text of the user message is null or empty. This results in an HTTP 400 error being returned from the Converse API, if a user message with only images but no text was sent, with the error message stating that there must be no empty text content block. Sending the same request without the empty text content block to the API via Postman results in a valid result.

**Environment**
Spring AI version: 2.0.0
Used Model Provider: Amazon Bedrock Converse API
Java version: 21 (Zulu JDK 21.48.16)

**Steps to reproduce**
1. Setup Spring AI to access a model like Claude Sonnet 4.6 via Amazon Bedrock.
2. Create a Prompt with a simple system message and one user message containing an empty text content (null is not allowed) and at least one image as media.
3. Call the Bedrock Chat Model with the prompt.

**Expected behavior**
There is no text content block created, the request is accepted by the API and a generation response is returned successfully.

**Minimal code example**
```
chatModel.call(
                    new Prompt(
                            List.of(
                                    SystemMessage.builder().text("Describe the image").build(),
                                    UserMessage.builder()
                                            .text("")
                                            .media(Media.builder()

```

title: Support configurable prompt cache TTL (1-hour) in Bedrock Converse `BedrockCacheOptions`
body:
**Expected Behavior**

`BedrockCacheOptions` should allow configuring the prompt cache TTL, so the
1-hour cache duration supported by Amazon Bedrock can be used through the
Bedrock Converse chat model — for example:

```java
BedrockCacheOptions.builder()
    .strategy(BedrockCacheStrategy.SYSTEM_ONLY)
    .multiBlockSystemCaching(true)
    .messageTypeTtl(MessageType.SYSTEM, BedrockCacheTtl.ONE_HOUR)
    .build();
```

This would mirror the API already available in the Anthropic module, where
`AnthropicCacheOptions` supports `messageTypeTtl(MessageType, AnthropicCacheTtl)`
with `FIVE_MINUTES` and `ONE_HOUR`. A single global `ttl` field on
`BedrockCacheOptions` would also cover the main use case.

**Current Behavior**

The Bedrock Converse prompt caching support always uses the default 5-minute
TTL. `BedrockCacheOptions` exposes `strategy` and `multiBlockSystemCaching`,
but no TTL setting, and the reference documentation states the TTL is fixed
at 5 minutes.

Amazon Bedrock, however, now supports a 1-hour TTL for prompt caching on
Anthropic Claude models (announced January 26, 2026, generally available in
all commercial AWS Regions):
https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/01/amazon-bedrock-one-hour-duration-prompt-caching

Anthropic's prompt caching documentation also lists the 1-hour cache duration
as available on Amazon Bedrock:
https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching

Because the option is not exposed, the extended TTL cannot be used through
the Bedrock Converse module.

**Context**

Use case: a multi-turn conversational application with a large static system
prompt (~1,500 tokens) cached via `SYSTEM_ONLY` + `multiBlockSystemCaching(true)`.
Users frequently pause more than 5 minutes between messages, so the cache
expires mid-session and each resumption pays the cache-write cost again. The
Anthropic module resolves this with `AnthropicCacheTtl.ONE_HOUR`; on Bedrock
Converse the extended TTL cannot be used.

Workaround considered: calling the provider SDK directly (Anthropic Java SDK
with the Bedrock backend) exposes `cache_control` with `"ttl": "1h"`, but
bypasses the module's cache strategy handling (`SYSTEM_ONLY`,
`multiBlockSystemCaching`, breakpoint placement).

Notes for implementation:

- Bedrock bills the 1-hour cache write at a different rate than the 5-minute
  write (2x base input vs 1.25x), so the TTL should remain opt-in with
  5 minutes as the default, matching current behavior.
- AWS documents 1-hour TTL availability per model, so passing the TTL through
  and letting the service validate model support seems preferable to
  client-side gating.

See #4872 (property-based configuration of `BedrockCacheOptions`) — if a TTL
option is added, it should be included in that property mapping as well.

[Bug] ToolSearchTool inputSchema parameter names degrade to arg0/arg1/arg2 (module not compiled with -parameters)
body:
### Environment
- `spring-ai-tool-search-tool` `2.0.1-SNAPSHOT`

### Symptom
`ToolSearchTool.toolSearchTool(@ToolParam String query, @ToolParam(required = false) Integer maxResults, @ToolParam(required = false) String categoryFilter, ToolContext toolContext)` generates an `inputSchema` whose property names are `arg0`/`arg1`/`arg2` instead of `query`/`maxResults`/`categoryFilter`.

### Evidence
`javap -v` on the published class shows no `MethodParameters` attribute (only `LocalVariableTable` debug info), i.e. the module was compiled without `-parameters`. `MethodToolCallback` then falls back to positional parameter names.

### Impact
The tool definition sent to the model uses positional parameter names; the LLM has to infer semantics from `@ToolParam.description`, and invocations written with the intended names (e.g. `{"query": "..."}`) fail argument parsing. It also complicates testing and debugging.

The root `pom.xml` declares `-parameters` for `maven-compiler-plugin` under `pluginManagement`; modules that do not explicitly declare the plugin (e.g. `spring-ai-tool-search-tool`) do not inherit it, which is the likely cause.

title: [Bug] ToolCallingAdvisor executes tool calls against original options, breaking ToolSearchToolCallingAdvisor ("No ToolCallback found for tool name: toolSearchTool")
body:
### Environment
- Spring AI `2.0.1-SNAPSHOT` (current `spring-ai-client-chat` snapshot)
- OpenAI-compatible streaming
- `ToolSearchToolCallingAdvisor` with `conversationHistoryEnabled(false)` and a custom `ToolCallingManager` backed by `StaticToolCallbackResolver`

### Symptom
When the model calls the internal `toolSearchTool`, execution fails:

```
java.lang.IllegalStateException: No ToolCallback found for tool name: toolSearchTool
    at org.springframework.ai.model.tool.DefaultToolCallingManager.executeToolCall(DefaultToolCallingManager.java:265) ~[spring-ai-model-2.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar:2.0.1-SNAPSHOT]
    at org.springframework.ai.model.tool.DefaultToolCallingManager.executeToolCalls(DefaultToolCallingManager.java:164) ~[spring-ai-model-2.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar:2.0.1-SNAPSHOT]
    at org.springframework.ai.chat.client.advisor.ToolCallingAdvisor.lambda$handleToolCallRecursion$6(ToolCallingAdvisor.java:350) ~[spring-ai-client-chat-2.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar:2.0.1-SNAPSHOT]
    at reactor.core.publisher.FluxDeferContextual.subscribe(FluxDeferContextual.java:50) ~[reactor-core-3.8.5.jar:3.8.5]
    at reactor.core.publisher.FluxSubscribeOn$SubscribeOnSubscriber.run(FluxSubscribeOn.java:197) ~[reactor-core-3.8.5.jar:3.8.5]
    at reactor.core.scheduler.BoundedElasticThreadPerTaskScheduler$SchedulerTask.run(BoundedElasticThreadPerTaskScheduler.java:1016) ~[reactor-core-3.8.5.jar:3.8.5]
    at java.base/java.lang.VirtualThread.run(VirtualThread.java:329) ~[na:na]
```

### Minimal reproduction
```java
ToolIndex toolIndex = new RegexToolIndex();

ChatClient chatClient = ChatClient.builder(chatModel) // any OpenAI-compatible streaming model
    .defaultTools(myToolA, myToolB)                   // per-bot tools, indexed per session
    .defaultAdvisors(SessionMemoryAdvisor.builder(sessionService).build())
    .defaultAdvisors(ToolSearchToolCallingAdvisor.builder()
        .toolIndex(toolIndex)
        .conversationHistoryEnabled(false)
        .build())
    .build();

chatClient.prompt()
    .user("find a calendar tool and create an event")
    .stream()
    .chatResponse()
    .toStream()
    .forEach(System.out::println);
```

Round 1 the model returns a tool call to the advisor-internal tool `toolSearchTool` (e.g. arguments `{"query": "calendar"}`). Executing that call throws the `IllegalStateException` above — with a real model you hit it on the first `toolSearchTool` invocation.

**Note:** `conversationHistoryEnabled(false)` and `SessionMemoryAdvisor` are **not** required to reproduce — the failure occurs on the first round regardless, because `prepareIteration` seeds every iteration's options with `toolSearchTool`.

### Root cause
Commit `029af3796` ("Add configurable tool call limits") changed which prompt/options `ToolCallingAdvisor` passes to `toolCallingManager.executeToolCalls(...)`:

- Before: stream path used `finalRequest.prompt()` and call path used `processedChatClientRequest.prompt()` — the per-iteration request whose options had already been enriched by `doBeforeStream`/`doBeforeCall`.
- After: stream path uses `new Prompt(fullTurnHistory, optionsCopy)` (`ToolCallingAdvisor.java:350`) and call path uses `new Prompt(fullTurnHistory, toolCallingChatOptions)` (`ToolCallingAdvisor.java:174-175`) — the original options captured on entry.

`ToolSearchToolCallingAdvisor.prepareIteration()` (`ToolSearchToolCallingAdvisor.java:249`, `262-267`) puts the internal `toolSearchTool` callback and previously discovered tools into a *per-iteration copy* of the options that is only sent to the model. `DefaultToolCallingManager.executeToolCall` (`DefaultToolCallingManager.java:255-258`) resolves callbacks first from `prompt.getOptions().getToolCallbacks()` and then from the `toolCallbackResolver`; neither contains `toolSearchTool`, so resolution fails.

This is a general regression, not specific to `toolSearchTool`: any tool a `ToolAdvisor` injects into the iteration options at `doBeforeCall`/`doBeforeStream` becomes unresolvable at execution time.

The same root cause also drops `TOOL_SEARCH_TOOL_SESSION_ID_KEY` from the execution-time `ToolContext` (`buildToolContext`, `DefaultToolCallingManager.java:176-185`): `prepareIteration` sets it on the per-iteration options copy, but execution reads the original options. So `ToolSearchTool` would still fail on its session-id `Objects.requireNonNull(...)` (`ToolSearchTool.java:54`) even if callback resolution were fixed.

### Impact
Tool search is unusable on the current snapshot — every `toolSearchTool` call errors. An app-level workaround (extra resolver entry + explicit session-id in the request tool context) is currently required.

### Suggested fix
Build the execution prompt with the enriched per-iteration options instead of the entry-captured ones, keeping the complete-history change from `029af3796`:
- stream: `new Prompt(fullTurnHistory, finalRequest.prompt().getOptions())`
- call: `new Prompt(fullTurnHistory, processedChatClientRequest.prompt().getOptions())`

This restores the injected tool callbacks and their tool context to the executor.

@tzolov this looks related to the `fullTurnHistory` split introduced in `029af3796`; could you take a look?

`TikaDocumentReader` repeats previous text when `get()` is called more than once
body:
**Bug description**

`TikaDocumentReader` keeps its `ContentHandler` in a final field built once by the constructor, and `get()` parses into that same handler on every call. `BodyContentHandler` accumulates and nothing resets it, so a second `get()` returns the first extraction followed by the second. The `Metadata` field is shared the same way.

Whether this counts as a defect depends on whether the reader is meant to be used more than once, and that is what I would like to settle.

Arguments that repeated calls should work: `DocumentReader` extends `Supplier<List<Document>>`, and the sibling readers are safe to call again. `TextReader` and `JsonReader` re-read the resource on each call, and `MarkdownDocumentReader` builds a new `DocumentVisitor` per read. `TikaDocumentReader` is the one that keeps its accumulator in a field.

Argument the other way: the reference documentation example builds a new reader inside the method that reads, so following the docs you never reach this. Nothing states that the reader is single use either.

If single use is intended, saying so on the class would be enough. If repeated calls are meant to work, the handler and the metadata need to be per call. One thing to note for that path: the public constructor that takes a `ContentHandler` hands ownership to the caller, so an injected handler probably cannot be recreated.

**Environment**

Spring AI `main` at `c988e72`. The same code is on `1.1.x` and `1.0.x`, under `document-readers/tika-reader`.
Java 17.0.19. No vector store involved.

**Steps to reproduce**

Build a `TikaDocumentReader` over any supported document and call `get()` twice.

**Expected behavior**

The second call returns the same text as the first.

What happens instead: the second call returns the first text with the same text appended. Using `word-sample.docx` from the module test resources, the first call returns 9798 characters and the second returns 19596, and the second starts with the first.

**Minimal Complete Reproducible example**

Add to `TikaDocumentReaderTests`:

```java
@Test
void secondReadRepeatsTheFirstExtraction() {
    var reader = new TikaDocumentReader("classpath:/word-sample.docx");

    String first = reader.get().get(0).getText();
    String second = reader.get().get(0).getText();

    assertThat(second).isEqualTo(first);
}
```

comments.author: ViniciusKoiti
comments.body:
I'd argue repeated calls should work: since `DocumentReader` extends `Supplier<List<Document>>` and the sibling readers (`TextReader`, `JsonReader`, `MarkdownDocumentReader`) are all safe to call again, `TikaDocumentReader` keeping its accumulator in a final field looks like an inconsistency rather than intended single-use design.

If the maintainers agree, I'd propose the following fix:

1. Move the `ContentHandler` and `Metadata` creation out of the constructor and into `get()`, so each invocation parses into a fresh `BodyContentHandler` and `Metadata`.
2. For the public constructor that accepts a caller-provided `ContentHandler` (which can't be recreated per call, as noted above): introduce a new constructor accepting a `Supplier<ContentHandler>` so custom handlers can also be re-created per invocation, deprecate the instance-based constructor, and keep its current behavior documented in the Javadoc for backward compatibility.
3. Add regression tests: the `secondReadRepeatsTheFirstExtraction` case from this issue, plus one asserting `Metadata` doesn't leak between calls.

@wantaekchoi if you're not planning to take this one yourself, I'd be happy to submit the PR along those lines. Either way, curious to hear whether the team sees the multi-call contract as the intended behavior.

comments.author: wantaekchoi
comments.body: @ViniciusKoiti Thanks! I’d wait for the maintainers to clarify the intended behavior first. After that, I’m happy for either of us to pick it up.

comments.author: ikaitist
comments.body:
Hi @ViniciusKoiti and @wantaekchoi - if neither of you has started on this, I would like to pick it up.

Proposed fix: make get() re-entrant by parsing into a fresh BodyContentHandler(-1) and a fresh Metadata on every call, matching the reuse semantics of TextReader/JsonReader, and drop the shared mutable fields.

For the 3-arg constructor that accepts a custom ContentHandler, I see two options and would appreciate a maintainer call:

- Option A: deprecate the 3-arg constructor (custom handler injection is incompatible with a re-entrant contract).
- Option B: keep it, but document that the supplied handler is only used for the first extraction.

I will add a regression test calling get() twice and asserting the second result contains no duplicated text. Happy to adjust based on maintainer feedback.

ikaitist
ViniciusKoiti

title: Streaming `reasoningContent` is exposed as accumulated full text — no incremental API for SSE typewriter UX
body:
## Background

Spring AI **2.0.1**, `spring-ai-starter-model-openai`, streaming via `ChatClient.stream().chatResponse()` against an OpenAI-compatible gateway backed by DeepSeek.

Since #6373 (aligned streaming `reasoning_content` with non-streaming responses), every intermediate streamed chunk carries the **full accumulated reasoning text** in the chunk metadata (`metadata["reasoningContent"]`):

```java
String accumulatedReasoning = reasoningMap.merge(id + ":" + choice.index(),
        getReasoningContent(choice), String::concat);
// ...
REASONING_CONTENT, accumulatedReasoning
```

I understand the rationale (the final aggregated `AssistantMessage` must keep the complete reasoning for advisor/chat-memory replay, since providers like DeepSeek require `reasoning_content` on replayed assistant tool-call messages).

## Problem

Streaming the reasoning to a frontend via SSE with a typewriter effect is a first-class need (ChatGPT-style UX). But with the current API there is **no incremental reasoning surface**:

- `Flux<ChatResponse>` chunks expose only the accumulated full text under `metadata["reasoningContent"]` — the wire `delta.reasoning_content` is incremental, but it never reaches consumers.
- Consumers are forced to reconstruct deltas client-side by prefix-stripping the accumulated text (accumulate → splice → trim), which is fragile, duplicated across every app, and easy to get wrong (multi-round tool loops, stream restarts).

This mirrors #5910 (tool-call argument deltas are also swallowed by provider/framework aggregation — milestone 2.1.x).

## Expected

Please provide an official incremental reasoning API, e.g. any of:

1. A per-chunk **`reasoningDelta`** field (alongside the accumulated `reasoningContent`) on the streamed `AssistantMessage` — mirrors what Vercel AI SDK does with `reasoning-delta` parts and what OpenAI/DeepSeek already send on the wire.
2. Or a unified stream-event API covering both reasoning deltas and tool-call arg deltas (reuse the #5910 effort).
3. At minimum, document the behavior: "intermediate chunks expose accumulated reasoning; derive deltas yourself" and show a canonical example.

Until then, every Spring AI user building a reasoning-aware chat UI has to reinvent the prefix-strip workaround.

## Repro context

```java
// 2.0.1, OpenAiChatModel stream()
chatModel.stream(prompt)
    .doOnNext(res -> {
        String full = res.getResult().getOutput().getMetadata()
                         .get("reasoningContent").toString();
        // full grows: "The" -> "The user asks" -> "The user asks what day" ...
    });
```

Related: #5898, #6230, #6373, #6375, #5910.

comments.author: hbsjz-swl
comments.body: @catch6 I can reproduce this issue with Spring AI 2.0.1 GA in my application. The final answer streams token by token, but the reasoning content is delivered in large accumulated blocks instead of incremental updates. When I switch back to 2.0.1-SNAPSHOT, incremental reasoning output works again with the same application and provider. In my application, the reasoning content is forwarded to the frontend through SSE. The current GA behavior exposes cumulative reasoningContent rather than the actual reasoning delta, so a ChatGPT-style typewriter UI cannot be implemented reliably without reconstructing the delta by prefix-stripping. I think the best fix would be to expose both: cumulative reasoningContent, which is needed for replay, memory, and tool-call scenarios; incremental reasoningDelta, which is needed by streaming UI consumers. At minimum, documenting that reasoningContent is cumulative and providing a canonical prefix-diff example would help. A unified stream-event API for reasoning deltas and tool-call argument deltas would be even better. This looks like a compatibility regression or API gap introduced by the GA streaming aggregation behavior.

comments.body:
Just ran into this exact issue in production using Spring AI 2.0.1.

Because reasoningContent is being accumulated in the metadata rather than sent as a delta, it causes a terrible "stuttering" effect on our frontend UI when streaming the response.

For anyone else stuck on this right now, our temporary workaround is to keep track of the string length using a local state inside Flux.defer() and use .substring(lastLength) to manually extract the delta chunk before sending it to the client. It works, but it obviously feels pretty hacky.

Since models with extended thinking are becoming the new standard, would love to see a native delta event for reasoning in 2.1.x (similar to how text deltas work).

title: Feature Request: Using function tools with human in the loop approvals

comments.author: CryoThrust
CryoThrust
comments.body: The proposed extension points are valuable, especially for production agent UIs. One contract detail I would make explicit before implementation is approval binding: a decision should be tied to the exact toolCallId, tool name, canonical arguments, conversation/turn, and an expiry/version. Reusing an approval after arguments change would be unsafe.\n\nThe framework should also preserve the assistant tool-call order and emit one result per call, including a sanitized DENIED/EXPIRED result, while keeping listener failures isolated from execution. Approval should return a CompletionStage and honor cancellation so reactive request threads are never blocked. A small compatibility matrix covering streaming and non-streaming paths, partial batch approval, duplicate resume, changed arguments, timeout, and listener failure would make the behavior reviewable.

comments.author: CryoThrust
comments.body:
To make this implementable as a first framework slice, I would keep the approval API narrower than a full durable pause/resume system:

- `ToolApprovalRequest` should contain the canonical serialized arguments, `toolCallId`, conversation/turn identity, and an expiry/version.
- The handler may return an asynchronous `CompletionStage<Decision>`; the framework owns waiting, cancellation, and the recursive tool-loop continuation so reactive request threads are not blocked.
- At execution time the framework must compare the approved request snapshot with the request being executed. A changed tool name or canonical argument set requires a new decision; an old approval must never authorize a mutated call.
- Decisions are per call, with `DENY`/expiry converted into one sanitized tool response per original call, preserving provider-required ordering. Listener/telemetry failures remain isolated from this path.

That gives applications a useful HITL integration point while leaving durable persistence and cross-instance resume as a later extension. A focused first PR could add the immutable request/decision types, a default-deny asynchronous gate, and contract tests for partial approval, changed arguments, duplicate completion, timeout/cancellation, and streaming versus non-streaming parity.

title: Per-call `customHeaders` not propagated in `OpenAiAudioTranscriptionOptions`, `OpenAiAudioSpeechOptions` and `OpenAiModerationOptions`
body:
**Bug description**

Per-call `customHeaders` are dropped by the remaining three affected OpenAI models: audio transcription, audio speech, and moderation.
[`OpenAiChatModel`](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-ai/blob/bf122ac7f92b805dd3391387004788456c5c03c6/models/spring-ai-openai/src/main/java/org/springframework/ai/openai/OpenAiChatModel.java#L847-L849) and [`OpenAiImageOptions`](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-ai/blob/bf122ac7f92b805dd3391387004788456c5c03c6/models/spring-ai-openai/src/main/java/org/springframework/ai/openai/OpenAiImageOptions.java#L214-L218) already propagate them; embeddings are covered by [#6574](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-ai/issues/6574) and its pending fix [#6575](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-ai/pull/6575).

**Root cause**

Each model merges the per-call options, then builds request params without reading `getCustomHeaders()`:

| Model | Request builder on `bf122ac7f` |
|---|---|
| Audio transcription | [`buildParams(...)`](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-ai/blob/bf122ac7f92b805dd3391387004788456c5c03c6/models/spring-ai-openai/src/main/java/org/springframework/ai/openai/OpenAiAudioTranscriptionModel.java#L187-L227) |
| Audio speech | [`buildSpeechCreateParams(...)`](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-ai/blob/bf122ac7f92b805dd3391387004788456c5c03c6/models/spring-ai-openai/src/main/java/org/springframework/ai/openai/OpenAiAudioSpeechModel.java#L266-L300) |
| Moderation | [`call(...)`](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-ai/blob/bf122ac7f92b805dd3391387004788456c5c03c6/models/spring-ai-openai/src/main/java/org/springframework/ai/openai/OpenAiModerationModel.java#L89-L115) |

The map is otherwise consumed only while constructing an internally managed client, as shown by [`OpenAiModerationModel`](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-ai/blob/bf122ac7f92b805dd3391387004788456c5c03c6/models/spring-ai-openai/src/main/java/org/springframework/ai/openai/OpenAiModerationModel.java#L64-L77) and [`OpenAiAudioTranscriptionModel.Builder`](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-ai/blob/bf122ac7f92b805dd3391387004788456c5c03c6/models/spring-ai-openai/src/main/java/org/springframework/ai/openai/OpenAiAudioTranscriptionModel.java#L384-L405). Per-call values therefore arrive after that read, and supplying an `OpenAIClient` skips it entirely.

The three `buildRequestOptions(...)` methods ([transcription](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-ai/blob/bf122ac7f92b805dd3391387004788456c5c03c6/models/spring-ai-openai/src/main/java/org/springframework/ai/openai/OpenAiAudioTranscriptionModel.java#L229-L241), [speech](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-ai/blob/bf122ac7f92b805dd3391387004788456c5c03c6/models/spring-ai-openai/src/main/java/org/springframework/ai/openai/OpenAiAudioSpeechModel.java#L302-L314), and [moderation](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-ai/blob/bf122ac7f92b805dd3391387004788456c5c03c6/models/spring-ai-openai/src/main/java/org/springframework/ai/openai/OpenAiModerationModel.java#L120-L132)) can set only the timeout because SDK [`RequestOptions`](https://github.com/openai/openai-java/blob/v4.49.0/openai-java-core/src/main/kotlin/com/openai/core/RequestOptions.kt#L5-L53) has no header field. The SDK instead exposes `putAdditionalHeader` on the [transcription](https://github.com/openai/openai-java/blob/v4.49.0/openai-java-core/src/main/kotlin/com/openai/models/audio/transcriptions/TranscriptionCreateParams.kt#L685-L692), [speech](https://github.com/openai/openai-java/blob/v4.49.0/openai-java-core/src/main/kotlin/com/openai/models/audio/speech/SpeechCreateParams.kt#L363-L370), and [moderation](https://github.com/openai/openai-java/blob/v4.49.0/openai-java-core/src/main/kotlin/com/openai/models/moderations/ModerationCreateParams.kt#L203-L210) params builders.

**Use case affected**

A gateway or proxy may require a header derived from each business request, which a static client-level header cannot express on a shared model bean.
This is the same use case as [#6082](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-ai/issues/6082) and [#5939](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-ai/issues/5939).

**Environment**

- Spring AI: `main` at `bf122ac7f` (`2.0.2-SNAPSHOT`), and 2.0.0
- module: `spring-ai-openai`
- openai-java: 4.49.0, as pinned by `openai-sdk.version` on `main`

**Steps to reproduce**

```java
ModerationResponse resp = openAiModerationModel.call(new ModerationPrompt("hi",
        OpenAiModerationOptions.builder()
            .customHeaders(Map.of("x-some-header-id", "VALUE_123"))
            .build()));
```

`x-some-header-id` is absent from the outgoing `/v1/moderations` request, and transcription and speech behave the same way.

**Expected behavior**

Per-call `customHeaders` are propagated as `additionalHeaders` on the params sent to the client, matching the chat and image semantics.

**Minimal Complete Reproducible Example**

This representative test fails on unmodified `main`; equivalent transcription and speech tests fail the same way:

```java
@Test
void moderationPropagatesPerCallCustomHeaders() {
    OpenAIClient mockClient = mock(OpenAIClient.class, RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS);
    when(mockClient.moderations().create(any(ModerationCreateParams.class), any(RequestOptions.class)))
        .thenReturn(ModerationCreateResponse.builder()
            .id("TEST_ID").model("TEST_MODEL").results(List.of()).build());

    OpenAiModerationModel model = OpenAiModerationModel.builder().openAiClient(mockClient).build();

    model.call(new ModerationPrompt("hi",
            OpenAiModerationOptions.builder()
                .customHeaders(Map.of("x-some-header-id", "VALUE_123"))
                .build()));

    ArgumentCaptor<ModerationCreateParams> captor = ArgumentCaptor.forClass(ModerationCreateParams.class);
    verify(mockClient.moderations()).create(captor.capture(), any(RequestOptions.class));
    assertThat(captor.getValue()._additionalHeaders().values("x-some-header-id"))
        .containsExactly("VALUE_123");
}
```

**Suggested fix**

Apply the same addition in all three request builders, matching the [`OpenAiImageOptions` fix from #6083](https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-ai/pull/6083/files):

```java
if (!CollectionUtils.isEmpty(options.getCustomHeaders())) {
    options.getCustomHeaders().forEach(builder::putAdditionalHeader);
}
```

comments.author: Haarris
comments.body:
One thing to watch with the approach in #6942. Each round moves the tool-result cachePoint to the newest tool message and drops the previous one. On Bedrock that breaks after a wide fan-out. A round with N parallel calls adds about 2N+1 content blocks (text, N toolUse, N toolResult), and Bedrock only looks back "approximately 20 content blocks" from a checkpoint to find an earlier entry (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-caching.html). pydantic-ai measured it in pydantic/pydantic-ai#9404: 10 parallel calls still hit, 11 read 0 and rewrote the whole conversation. I measured the same edge directly: 21 added blocks still hit, 22 always missed. The first-party Claude API doesn't have this problem because it counts a run of tool_use or tool_result blocks as one position; Bedrock counts every block.

Here the last-user-message checkpoint still hits, so the miss is partial, but every tool output since then gets written again. Under CONVERSATION_HISTORY you only use 2 of the 4 slots, so keeping a cachePoint on the previous tool result message too (or only when the new round adds 18+ blocks) would avoid it.

I made a small free tool that flags this when you diff two saved requests: https://github.com/Haarris/cachecanary

title: `InMemoryChatMemoryRepository` retains the caller's mutable message list
Bedrock Converse: tool-call arguments serialized via Document.toString() produce invalid JSON, breaking tool execution when arguments contain newlines
body:
### Bug description

When using the Bedrock Converse chat model with tool calling, `BedrockProxyChatModel` serializes the tool-use input by calling `toString()` on the AWS SDK `Document`:

https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-ai/blob/main/models/spring-ai-bedrock-converse/src/main/java/org/springframework/ai/bedrock/converse/BedrockProxyChatModel.java#L676

```java
var functionArguments = toolUseContentBlock.toolUse().input().toString();
```

`Document.toString()` is **not** a JSON serializer. It renders string values without escaping control characters (e.g. `\n`, `\t`). The resulting string is stored verbatim as `AssistantMessage.ToolCall#arguments`.

When the tool is executed, the arguments string is parsed back into a `Map` with a strict Jackson 3 mapper via the static `JsonHelper.fromJsonToMap(...)` (e.g. in `SyncMcpToolCallback`/`AsyncMcpToolCallback`). Jackson 3 rejects unescaped control characters inside string values, so the call fails:

```
tools.jackson.core.exc.StreamReadException: Illegal unquoted character
((CTRL-CHAR, code 10)): has to be escaped using backslash to be included in string value
 ... (through reference chain: java.util.LinkedHashMap["text"])
      at org.springframework.ai.util.JsonHelper.fromJsonToMap(JsonHelper.java)
      at org.springframework.ai.mcp.SyncMcpToolCallback.call(SyncMcpToolCallback.java)
      at org.springframework.ai.model.tool.DefaultToolCallingManager.executeToolCall(...)
```

The bug is latent for single-line tool arguments and only surfaces when the model puts a newline (or other control character) into a tool argument — which is common and natural, e.g. a multi-line message body passed to a `send`-style tool.

Because `JsonHelper` is a `static final` field on the tool-callback classes, there is no injection point to relax parsing on the consuming side — the defect must be fixed where the malformed string is produced.

### Environment

- Spring AI: 2.0.1 (also present on `main`)
- Module: `spring-ai-bedrock-converse`
- Jackson: 3.x (`tools.jackson.*`), strict about unescaped control characters by default
- Model: Anthropic Claude via Bedrock Converse (channel-agnostic; any tool with a string
  argument containing a newline reproduces it)

### Steps to reproduce

1. Configure a `ChatClient` with the Bedrock Converse model and any tool that accepts a string parameter.
2. Prompt the model so it calls the tool with a multi-line string argument (containing `\n`).
3. Tool execution fails with the `StreamReadException` above; the request returns a 500.

### Expected behavior

Tool-call arguments produced by `BedrockProxyChatModel` should be valid JSON regardless of the content of string values, so they round-trip through `JsonHelper.fromJsonToMap(...)` during tool execution.

### Root cause

`Document.toString()` is used as if it were a JSON serializer. The `Document` is a structured value (map/list/string/number/boolean/null) and should be serialized with a real JSON writer. Note the request path already does the correct inverse:
`ConverseApiUtils.convertObjectToDocument(jsonHelper.fromJsonToMap(toolCall.arguments()))`.

### Proposed fix

Add the inverse converter `ConverseApiUtils.convertDocumentToObject(Document)` and serialize with the existing `jsonHelper`:

```java
var functionArguments = jsonHelper
    .toJson(ConverseApiUtils.convertDocumentToObject(toolUseContentBlock.toolUse().input()));
```

This escapes control characters correctly, is symmetric with the request path, and fixes the issue for all tools (not just MCP).

### Alternatives considered

- **Relax JSON parsing to allow unescaped control characters** (e.g. enable `JsonReadFeature.ALLOW_UNESCAPED_CONTROL_CHARS` on the mapper used by `JsonHelper`, or  leniently re-parse the arguments before execution). Rejected as the upstream fix: it treats the symptom rather than the cause, weakens strict JSON parsing framework-wide (hiding malformed data elsewhere), and assumes `Document.toString()` is otherwise valid JSON, which is not a documented contract. It is only appropriate as a downstream workaround where the producing code cannot be changed (the static `JsonHelper` leaves no seam in the callback layer).

title: Groq GPT-OSS tool calling fails on subsequent request because reasoning_content is replayed by ToolCallingAdvisor
body:
## Bug description

When using Spring AI 2.0.0 with Groq's OpenAI-compatible API and `openai/gpt-oss-120b`, a tool-calling request can fail on the second model invocation because `reasoningContent` from the first `AssistantMessage` is replayed as `reasoning_content` in the subsequent request.

The first model invocation succeeds. GPT-OSS returns both reasoning information and a tool call. Spring AI then executes the tool through `ToolCallingAdvisor` and constructs the next model request using the conversation history.

The problem occurs because the previous `AssistantMessage` still contains `reasoningContent`. When the history is serialized by `OpenAiChatModel`, this becomes `reasoning_content` in the assistant message sent to Groq.

Groq rejects this field in the subsequent request:

```text
400: 'messages.6' : for 'role:assistant' ...
property 'reasoning_content' is unsupported
```

### Environment

* Spring AI: `2.0.0`
* Spring Boot: `4.1.0`
* Java: `21`
* Model provider: Groq
* Model: `openai/gpt-oss-120b`
* API: Groq OpenAI-compatible API
* Tool calling: `ToolCallingAdvisor`
* Invocation: non-streaming `ChatClient.call()`

### Configuration

The model is configured using the OpenAI-compatible Spring AI integration:

```properties
spring.ai.openai.api-key=${GROQ_API_KEY}
spring.ai.openai.base-url=https://api.groq.com/openai/v1
spring.ai.openai.chat.model=openai/gpt-oss-120b
```

I also tested Groq's `include_reasoning=false` option:

```java
OpenAiChatOptions.builder()
    .model("openai/gpt-oss-120b")
    .extraBody(Map.of("include_reasoning", false))
    .build();
```

However, the `AssistantMessage` produced during the tool-calling flow still contains `reasoningContent`, and the subsequent request still fails when that message is replayed.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Configure Spring AI 2.0.0 to use Groq's OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
2. Use `openai/gpt-oss-120b`.
3. Register a simple tool, for example:

```java
@Tool
public String getCurrentTime(String timeZone) {
    // return current time
}
```

4. Ask the model a question that requires the tool.
5. GPT-OSS returns an assistant response containing:

   * `reasoningContent`
   * a `tool_call`
6. `ToolCallingAdvisor` executes the tool.
7. Spring AI constructs the next request using the conversation history.
8. The previous assistant message is serialized with `reasoning_content`.
9. Groq returns HTTP 400 because `reasoning_content` is unsupported in the request.

### Observed flow

The relevant flow appears to be:

```text
User request
    ↓
OpenAiChatModel → Groq
    ↓
Assistant response
    ├── reasoningContent
    └── tool_call
    ↓
ToolCallingAdvisor
    ↓
Tool execution
    ↓
Conversation history
    ↓
AssistantMessage containing reasoningContent
    ↓
OpenAiChatModel serializes history
    ↓
reasoning_content
    ↓
Groq HTTP 400
```

The first request itself does not contain `reasoning_content`. The field is introduced into the subsequent request when the previous `AssistantMessage` is replayed.

### Expected behavior

Spring AI should be able to complete the tool-calling loop with providers whose OpenAI-compatible request schema does not accept `reasoning_content`.

Ideally, reasoning information should remain available in Spring AI's internal `AssistantMessage` representation while its serialization into subsequent provider requests should respect the requirements/capabilities of the target provider/model.

### Related reasoning-content behavior

There are existing Spring AI issues concerning the opposite situation, where reasoning content must be replayed to providers such as DeepSeek.

For example, DeepSeek reasoning models require `reasoning_content` to be passed back in subsequent requests. Therefore, simply removing reasoning information from `AssistantMessage` globally would likely break providers that require it.

This suggests that the problem may be related to how provider-specific reasoning information is mapped when assistant history is reconstructed for subsequent requests.

### Workaround

I was able to prevent this specific Groq failure by extending `ToolCallingAdvisor` and removing `reasoningContent` from the assistant message before the next tool-calling iteration.

Conceptually:

```text
AssistantMessage
    reasoningContent
    toolCalls
        ↓
ToolCallingAdvisor
        ↓
remove reasoningContent for Groq
        ↓
next request
```

This prevents the invalid `reasoning_content` field from being sent to Groq while preserving the tool call and conversation history.

### Possible area to investigate

The relevant interaction appears to be between:

* `ToolCallingAdvisor`
* `AssistantMessage`
* `OpenAiChatModel`
* OpenAI-compatible provider-specific request serialization

The key question seems to be whether reasoning content should be serialized unconditionally when rebuilding assistant history, or whether provider/model-specific behavior should determine whether `reasoning_content` is included.

I would be happy to provide a minimal reproducible project and work on a PR if this is considered an appropriate fix for Spring AI.

title: Add VectorStore.upsert for pre-computed embeddings
body:
Every vector store embeds inside `add()`, so there's no way to write vectors you
  already have (for e.g, from an overnight batch API, another team's pipeline, a migration
  that exports text and vectors together, or a multimodal model over an image/video, etc.)

  So a small, additive method:

  ```
  public record EmbeddedDocument(Document document, float[] embedding) { }

  // VectorStore
  default void upsert(List<EmbeddedDocument> entries) {
      throw new UnsupportedOperationException(getName() + " does not support upsert");
  }
```
  The default throws an exception, so stores that don't implement it are unaffected, and
  add()/Document stay untouched. Same id replaces the row, so re-running with stable ids won't duplicate. Instrumented stores get a `doUpsert` on `AbstractObservationVectorStore` and an UPSERT operation, so it shows up in metrics. 

  For content that lives elsewhere (an image in S3, a doc too big for the row), a new
  `DocumentMetadata.CONTENT_REF` key holds the pointer. The store never reads it; the
  app resolves it after search.

 Scoped for 2.1.0-M1:

  - [ ] EmbeddedDocument + VectorStore.upsert
  - [ ] observation wiring
  - [ ] CONTENT_REF
  - [ ] pgvector + a shared test suite others reuse (Testcontainers only)
  - [ ] Redis, Elasticsearch, Qdrant
  - [ ] docs

  Later: the rest of the stores (Milvus does a plain insert and Bedrock KB has no
  write path, so those are the awkward ones), and deterministic ids / clean re-runs 
  (upsert is what those build on)

  Closes #3540. Replaces #3541 (which changed the doAdd signature) with an additive
  path — thanks @aniketg-21, the pair object came from there. Also helps #1009: embed
  multimodally yourself, then upsert the vector.
